title: Facade
summary: Offer one simple operation in front of a subsystem the caller should not orchestrate.

parts.rule: A facade exposes a small, intention-revealing operation over a subsystem with several collaborators. The facade owns the normal call order and default choices; callers ask for an outcome instead of assembling the subsystem themselves. The underlying classes can remain available for clients that truly need lower-level control.
parts.why: When every caller repeats the same five-step ritual, the sequence drifts: one forgets cleanup, another reverses two calls, and a third picks a different default. A facade gives that common path one implementation. Its danger is scope creep—a facade that absorbs every business capability becomes a god object rather than a boundary.
parts.example: A checkout controller needs to place an order for 2 units of item 42 at $30 each. Without a facade it might call Inventory.reserve(), Payments.authorize(), Orders.insert(), and Events.publish() in four controllers. CheckoutFacade.placeOrder(command) makes that sequence explicit. First it validates an idempotency key, then reserves 2 units, authorizes 6000 cents, writes order 781, and publishes OrderPlaced(781). It returns an OrderReceipt rather than exposing the four subsystem clients. If authorization fails, the facade releases the reservation and returns PaymentDeclined; if the order already exists for the idempotency key, it returns the earlier receipt. Inventory still owns stock rules and Payments still owns authorization—the facade coordinates them but does not reimplement them. A batch-import tool that must reserve 500 items before one payment may use the lower-level APIs because its workflow is genuinely different. Tests for the web controller can fake CheckoutFacade with one operation, while integration tests exercise the full order sequence and compensation. Calling Orders.insert() through a method named placeOrder() with no other work would not earn a facade; that would only rename a single call.
parts.use: Use a facade at a module boundary when several callers need the same multi-step workflow or safe defaults. Give it methods named for user or domain intentions, keep the surface narrow, and leave detailed calculations with the collaborators that own them. It is especially useful when subsystem internals change more often than caller needs.
parts.refuse: Skip a facade that only forwards one method under a new name. Do not collect unrelated workflows into one ApplicationFacade. Avoid hiding important customization that real clients need; provide explicit options or documented lower-level access instead. A facade simplifies access, but it does not make partial failure, transactions, or compensation disappear.

body:
Rule. A facade exposes a small, intention-revealing operation over a subsystem with several collaborators. The facade owns the normal call order and default choices; callers ask for an outcome instead of assembling the subsystem themselves. The underlying classes can remain available for clients that truly need lower-level control.

Why it matters. When every caller repeats the same five-step ritual, the sequence drifts: one forgets cleanup, another reverses two calls, and a third picks a different default. A facade gives that common path one implementation. Its danger is scope creep—a facade that absorbs every business capability becomes a god object rather than a boundary.

Worked example. A checkout controller needs to place an order for 2 units of item 42 at $30 each. Without a facade it might call Inventory.reserve(), Payments.authorize(), Orders.insert(), and Events.publish() in four controllers. CheckoutFacade.placeOrder(command) makes that sequence explicit. First it validates an idempotency key, then reserves 2 units, authorizes 6000 cents, writes order 781, and publishes OrderPlaced(781). It returns an OrderReceipt rather than exposing the four subsystem clients. If authorization fails, the facade releases the reservation and returns PaymentDeclined; if the order already exists for the idempotency key, it returns the earlier receipt. Inventory still owns stock rules and Payments still owns authorization—the facade coordinates them but does not reimplement them. A batch-import tool that must reserve 500 items before one payment may use the lower-level APIs because its workflow is genuinely different. Tests for the web controller can fake CheckoutFacade with one operation, while integration tests exercise the full order sequence and compensation. Calling Orders.insert() through a method named placeOrder() with no other work would not earn a facade; that would only rename a single call.

[[diagram:facade]]

When to use. Use a facade at a module boundary when several callers need the same multi-step workflow or safe defaults. Give it methods named for user or domain intentions, keep the surface narrow, and leave detailed calculations with the collaborators that own them. It is especially useful when subsystem internals change more often than caller needs.

When to refuse. Skip a facade that only forwards one method under a new name. Do not collect unrelated workflows into one ApplicationFacade. Avoid hiding important customization that real clients need; provide explicit options or documented lower-level access instead. A facade simplifies access, but it does not make partial failure, transactions, or compensation disappear.
